title: Punjab Police Officers Charged With Fabricating a Dead Man's Testimony in NRI Woman's Murder Case
excerpt: A witness statement recorded four months after the witness died exposes deep rot in the investigation of a US-based Sikh woman's gruesome killing in Ludhiana
body:
The murder of Rupinder Kaur Pandher was already one of the most disturbing NRI crime stories to emerge from Punjab in years. A 72-year-old American citizen of Indian origin, she flew from Seattle to Ludhiana in the summer of 2025, lured by a marriage proposal from a UK-based NRI named Charanjit Singh Grewal. She never returned. Her body, burned on coal for two days and dumped in a drain, was found only after her sister filed a missing person's complaint.

Now the case has taken an even darker turn. Punjab Police have registered an FIR against two of their own officers — former Dehlon Station House Officer Sukhjinder Singh and head constable Sanjiv Kumar — for fabricating a witness statement from a man who had been dead for nearly four months when his supposed testimony was recorded.

## Context and Background

Rupinder Kaur, a divorcee based in the United States, had connected with Grewal through a matrimonial platform. Before travelling to India, she transferred approximately fifty lakh rupees to him. Upon arrival in Ludhiana, she was murdered — allegedly on Grewal's orders — by Sukhjeet Singh, a local court typist who confessed to bludgeoning her with a baseball bat on 12 July 2025. The body was burned and the remains disposed of in a local drain.

Police arrested Sukhjeet Singh relatively quickly. But Grewal, identified as the alleged mastermind, remained abroad. Sukhjeet's brother Manvir Singh, also named in the case, went into hiding. When Manvir approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court seeking anticipatory bail, his petition contained an explosive allegation: a witness statement attributed to one Gurpreet Singh, dated 19 September 2025, had been fabricated. Gurpreet Singh had died on 29 May 2025 — nearly four months before the police claimed to have recorded his testimony.

## Current Developments

The High Court took cognisance of the allegation, prompting the registration of a fresh FIR against the two officers under sections relating to evidence tampering, fabrication of documents, and distortion of official records. The investigation is ongoing and additional charges may follow.

This is not an isolated procedural error. Recording a statement from a deceased individual suggests a deliberate attempt to bolster the prosecution's case with manufactured evidence — a practice that, if left unchecked, could have secured wrongful convictions or allowed the real conspirators to evade justice.

The FIR also encompasses broader irregularities in the original investigation, including questions about how the case was handled in its early stages. Legal analysts in Chandigarh say the case raises systemic concerns about evidence integrity in Punjab's police apparatus, particularly in cases involving NRI victims where families are often thousands of miles away and unable to monitor proceedings closely.

## Diaspora Impact

For the estimated two million Punjabi-origin NRIs living in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, the case strikes at a persistent fear: that the Indian justice system cannot be trusted to protect them or their families when crimes occur on Indian soil. Matrimonial fraud targeting elderly NRIs is a well-documented phenomenon in Punjab, where elaborate schemes involving fake identities, forged Aadhaar cards, and cross-border financial manipulation have ensnared dozens of victims in recent years.

The fabrication of evidence by investigating officers adds a deeply troubling dimension. If the police themselves cannot be relied upon to build honest cases, the families of NRI victims face a justice system stacked against them at every level — from crime to courtroom.

Diaspora advocacy groups have long called for dedicated NRI policing cells with independent oversight. The Pandher case may finally force Punjab's government to act.

## What Comes Next

The investigation into the two officers is now under judicial scrutiny. Legal observers expect the High Court to demand periodic status reports. Manvir Singh's anticipatory bail petition remains pending, and the larger question of Charanjit Singh Grewal's extradition from the United Kingdom has yet to be resolved.

For Rupinder Kaur's family in Seattle, justice remains distant. The woman who crossed an ocean seeking companionship found death instead — and the institution tasked with finding the truth chose to fabricate it.
